content: Gamma (uppercase Γ, lowercase γ) is the third letter of the Greek alphabet. In the Greek numeral system, it holds a numerical value of 3. The letter Gamma originated from the Phoenician letter Gimel. Over time, Gamma gave rise to other letters, including the Roman letters C and G, as well as the Cyrillic letters Ge (Г) and Ghe (Ґ). In Modern Greek, Gamma represents either a voiced velar fricative [ɣ] or a voiced palatal fricative [ʝ], depending on the phonetic context. In Ancient Greek, however, it represented a voiced velar stop [ɡ]. When it appears before velar consonants, Gamma represents a velar nasal [ŋ] in both Modern and Ancient Greek. Additionally, a double Gamma (γγ) represents a prenasalized voiced velar stop [ŋɡ]. Gamma Combinations Gamma can combine with other letters or with itself to produce specific pronunciations: A double Gamma (γγ) is pronounced like the ng in the English word jumping. A Gamma followed by Xi (γξ) is pronounced roughly like the nx in the word Sphinx. A Gamma followed by Chi (γχ) is pronounced like the nkh in the word ankh. A Gamma combined with Kappa (γκ) is pronounced like the nk in the word banker. Use as a Symbol or Term Gamma is frequently used as a symbol to denote variables in mathematics and physics. In specific contexts, it carries specialized meanings. For example, in nuclear physics, Gamma represents gamma radiation, while in the theory of relativity, it denotes the Lorentz factor. In mathematics, the Gamma function (commonly written as the Γ-function) is a significant concept.
